nameStory: This plant gets its common name 'Fortune's spindle' from Robert Fortune, a Scottish botanist who collected plants in Asia in the 1800s and introduced many species to Western gardens. The 'spindle' part refers to the hard wood that was traditionally used to make spindles for spinning thread, a characteristic shared with other plants in the Euonymus genus.
description: Fortune's spindle is a versatile evergreen vine or groundcover that can climb up trees and structures or spread along the ground. It produces small, leathery leaves that stay green year-round and can grow quite vigorously, sometimes covering large areas. This Asian native has become widely planted as an ornamental but has proven to be highly invasive in New England forests.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves about 1-2 inches long with slightly toothed edges and a waxy, leathery feel. They're arranged in opposite pairs along the stem and stay green through winter, though they may take on purplish tones in cold weather.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Can grow as either a climbing vine using small rootlets to grip bark and walls, or as a spreading groundcover mat. The stems are flexible and green when young, becoming woody with age.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish-white flowers with 4 petals appear in late spring. They're so small you might miss them, but they cluster along the stems and have a faint, sweet scent.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small pinkish capsules split open to reveal bright orange seeds in fall, though fruiting is uncommon in New England. The colorful seeds are eye-catching against the dark green foliage.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: On older climbing stems, the bark becomes grayish-brown and develops a slightly corky texture. You can often see small aerial rootlets that help the vine cling to surfaces.

habitat: Originally planted in gardens and landscaping, Fortune's spindle has escaped to colonize forest edges, woodland understories, and disturbed areas throughout New England. It thrives in both sunny and shady locations and tolerates a wide range of soil conditions. You'll often find it climbing up native trees in suburban woodlands and parks.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges bright green, and tiny flowers appear in late spring. This is when the plant puts on its most vigorous growth.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain consistently green and leathery. The plant continues to spread and climb actively during warm weather.
seasonality.fall: Rare fruit capsules may appear, splitting to show bright orange seeds. Leaves may develop purple tinges as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen leaves persist but often turn purplish or bronze in cold weather. The waxy leaves and woody stems remain easily identifiable.

funFact: Fortune's spindle is so good at climbing that it can completely engulf and eventually kill mature trees by blocking their sunlight - some specimens have been found climbing over 60 feet high into forest canopies, creating what look like giant green cocoons around dead trees.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other evergreen vines like English ivy, but Fortune's spindle has opposite leaves (ivy's are alternate) and a more leathery texture. Remember: opposite leaves and waxy feel = Fortune's spindle.
contextualKnowledge: Though widely sold and planted as 'wintercreeper' for groundcover, this species is increasingly recognized as a serious invasive threat to New England forests. Many states now discourage or prohibit its sale, and removal is recommended to protect native ecosystems.
compareHints: Unlike winged euonymus (burning bush) which is deciduous with prominent corky wing-like ridges on stems, Fortune's spindle stays evergreen and has smooth, round stems. While other Euonymus species in New England grow as shrubs, Fortune's spindle is unique in its ability to vine and climb extensively.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Euonymus relatives in New England, winged euonymus is the only one with prominent corky wings on the stems.
Unlike its notorious relative winged euonymus (burning bush), European spindle lacks the prominent corky 'wings' on its stems and has much less intense fall leaf color.
American wahoo differs from its cousin winged euonymus (burning bush) by lacking the distinctive corky wings on its stems and being much less common.
Among New England's euonymus species, Hamilton's spindle stands out for its four-lobed pink fruits and dangling orange seeds on threads.

Large-leaved spindle stands out from its New England relatives primarily by leaf size – its leaves are significantly larger than the small leaves of winged euonymus or the narrow leaves of other spindle species.
Unlike its deciduous relatives like winged euonymus (burning bush) or wahoo, Japanese spindle keeps its leaves year-round.
